title: Operator-limited-retention: sanitized audit slivers and change-envelope API (PRD - rough)
body:
Purpose:
This PRD proposes a small-surface feature: Operator-limited retention for customer-managed networking changes implemented as "sanitized audit slivers" and a compact, attestable change-envelope API. Goal is to give customers and their auditors a reliable cryptographic proof-of-change while minimizing retention of sensitive configuration payloads on Redwood side, reducing risk and compliance burden for private deployments.

Problem statement:
- Customers require immutable evidence of network changes (VPC peering, firewall rules, route table updates) for audits and incident investigations.
- Many changes contain sensitive details (internal IP ranges, hostnames, keys) that customers do not want stored indefinitely in the Redwood control plane or exported to ops teams.
- Current options (full audit retention or aggressive redaction) force a tradeoff: either retain sensitive data for long periods (risk) or lose fidelity necessary for post-incident forensic analysis (compliance risk).

Proposal summary:
- Introduce a compact change-envelope API that produces: (a) a minimal "audit sliver" — cryptographically hashed, policy-sanitized metadata about a change; (b) an optional encrypted blob containing the full change payload that is customer-escrowed (or optionally stored encrypted by Redwood with strict TTL and KMS policies).
- Audit slivers are signed by Redwood and include Merkle-rooted references that can be used later to verify integrity of a full payload provided by the customer or escrow. Slivers contain only non-sensitive fields plus a deterministic fingerprint of the sensitive fields.
- Provide retention tiers: operator-ephemeral (30 days), legal-hold (extendable by customer), and customer-escrow-only (Redwood never stores plaintext).

Key user personas:
- Platform engineer at a regulated customer: needs an auditable trail to satisfy SOC2/ISO during quarterly audits without exposing sensitive hostnames to vendor ops.
- Operator/Redwood SRE: needs enough metadata to correlate incidents with service telemetry but must not have access to secrets or PII without customer consent.
- Security/compliance reviewer: needs verifiable proof that a change occurred and that evidence is authentic and unmodified.

Requirements (MUST):
- API: Create/Commit/Query endpoints for change-envelope objects. Create returns a signed audit sliver (JSON) and an envelope-id.
- Cryptography: Slivers must include a timestamp, actor-id, change-type, non-sensitive diff summary, and a deterministic fingerprint (SHA-256) of the redacted sensitive blob. Redwood signs slivers using the control-plane signing key; signature metadata returned for verifier use.
- Escrow options: customer-managed escrow (S3/GCS with provided URL + proof-of-possession) or Redwood-encrypted escrow with customer-controlled KMS key.
- Retention controls: per-customer policy config (default: operator-ephemeral 30d). Legal-hold flag can be set by customer. Redwood cannot override customer-escrow retention.
- Verification: API to fetch sliver and verify signature; if customer provides the full payload, a Merkle/MAC path can be computed to prove match of fingerprint.

Requirements (SHOULD):
- Console: UI showing recent slivers, retention state, and quick links to start an escrow export.
- Forensic helper: a small CLI utility (or SDK helper) to assemble escrowed payloads and verify against sliver proofs locally.
- Audit export format: ndjson or compact JSON lines; include slivers and optional signed tokens proving Redwood issued the sliver.

Non-goals:
- We are not building a full eDiscovery pipeline or long-term forensic archive in this iteration.
- We will not provide an inter-op standard for third-party escrow services beyond common S3-compatible storage and signed URLs.

Architecture notes:
- Change-envelope is produced at the conclusion of an operator action (e.g., API-driven VPC change or on-prem network handshake). The control-plane generates two outputs: sliver and encrypted-blob-reference. Sliver stored in lightweight append-only index (compact metadata DB).
- Signing: control-plane key is rotated per Redwood KMS practice; historical slivers include key-id to trace signature.
- Escrow verification uses either the customer-provided symmetric key (for Redwood-encrypted escrow) to decrypt payload or a customer-supplied URL + HMAC proof to fetch directly from customer storage during verification.

API sketch (proto-style in text):
- POST /v1/private/change-envelopes
  body: {actor, target, diff, sensitive_blob_optional, escrow_preference}
  returns: {envelope_id, sliver_json, sliver_signature}
- GET /v1/private/change-envelopes/{id}/sliver -> returns sliver + signature + retention_state
- POST /v1/private/change-envelopes/{id}/verify -> body: {candidate_payload or escrow_proof} -> returns verification status true/false + diagnostic log

Console UX (rough):
- Per-customer panel: retention slider (30d / 90d / customer-escrow-only / legal-hold).
- Change detail page shows sliver (human readable), signature verification status, and a "request escrow payload" workflow (auditor token generation, one-time link, or KMS handshake).

Acceptance criteria:
- Unit/integration tests for sliver generation, signature verification, and retention lifecycle transitions.
- Demo scenario: simulate a VPC route change; produce sliver, store encrypted escrow to customer bucket, and demonstrate local verification using CLI.
- Policy test: show that when retention set to operator-ephemeral, Redwood deletes any plaintext-encrypted payload after TTL but retains signed sliver.

Open questions / risks:
- Legal: does a cryptographic sliver without full payload meet evidentiary standards in target jurisdictions? Need legal signoff per-region.
- Cost: escrow storage and retrieval in verification flows may have cost implications; must model expected rate of auditor requests.
- UX: customers may be confused by multiple retention knobs (operator, escrow, legal-hold). Need clear defaults and guardrails.
- Attacks: ensure fingerprinting approach is resilient to substitution attacks (use Merkle trees + nonces). Decide whether to include salted fingerprints per-change.

Implementation plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (2w): design spec and legal review; prototype sliver JSON shape and signing flow.
- Phase 1 (4w): API + signing + local CLI verification; minimal in-memory index and manual escrow (pre-signed URLs).
- Phase 2 (6w): integrate Redwood KMS-based encrypted escrow, retention job, Console UI, and RBAC checks.
- Phase 3 (2w): pilot with 1–2 customers (SaaS pilot), collect feedback and adjust defaults.

Telemetry & SLOs:
- Metric: sliver-generation latency, verify-latency, escrow-download-latency, number of legal-holds.
- SLO: sliver generation < 300ms p95 for hosted control-plane operations.

Backwards compat / migration:
- Existing audit logs remain available. For new change events, emit slivers alongside current logs until customers opt-in to sliver-only retention. Migration guide to be documented.

Appendix: example sliver JSON (readable):
{
  "envelope_id": "env-20241105-00021",
  "timestamp": "2024-11-05T18:32:21Z",
  "actor": "platform-admin@example.com",
  "change_type": "route-update",
  "target": "cust-12345/vpc-7b2f",
  "non_sensitive_summary": "added route 10.20.0.0/16 -> transit-gw",
  "fingerprint": "sha256:3f1a...",
  "merkle_root": "sha256:9d2b...",
  "signing_key_id": "cp-key-v2",
  "signature": "base64(...)"
}

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus review on the legal/forensic acceptability and the UX semantics of retention tiers. Engineering should comment on cost assumptions for escrow verification. Security should validate the proposed fingerprint/merkle approach.

Next steps:
- Schedule cross-functional review with Legal + Security (target 2024-11-18).
- Build Phase 0 prototype branch and run tabletop verification use cases with Solutions Eng.

- Asha
